p.x:
My sister Fah is sixteen, and she loves social media. Every day, she posts pictures of her food, her friends and, of course, herself. She takes at least ten selfies before she chooses one to post with a few words! She gets lots of likes, and her friends write comments with emojis like hearts and smiling faces.
Fah has about 2,000 followers. Most of them are friends from school, but some are strangers. My parents were worried, so they asked her to change her profile from public to private. Now only people she knows can follow her.
Fah also uses a group chat with her classmates. They share homework, news and links to funny videos. Sometimes she sends me a link too, but I'm usually too busy to click on it! My mother says Fah spends too much time online, but Fah says, "It's how I talk to my friends."

p.t: Why Do Some Videos Go Viral?
p.x:
Every day, millions of videos are uploaded, but only a few go viral. What makes the difference? Researchers who study online content say there are some common patterns.
First, emotion matters. Videos that make people laugh, cry or feel surprised are shared much more than neutral ones. Second, timing is important. Creators often post when their audience is most active, usually in the evening, when people are scrolling through their phones after work. Third, a clever hashtag can help a video reach people far beyond the creator's own followers, especially if it becomes part of a trend.
Many successful creators started small. Some began by writing a blog, then started a video channel and asked readers to subscribe. They reply to comments, tag other users in their posts, and choose a short, memorable username. But going viral has a downside too: sudden attention can attract unkind messages, and some creators have had to block hundreds of accounts.

Social media influencers are now a powerful force in marketing. Brands pay them to promote products, measuring success not only by the number of followers but also by engagement: how many people like, comment on and share each post. Some influencers earn more from a single post than many workers do in a year.
Critics argue that influencer culture presents an unrealistic image of life. Influencers carefully curate their feeds, posting only the best moments and often using a filter to change their appearance. Psychologists warn that young users who compare themselves with these images may feel inadequate, and that the constant search for validation through likes can damage self-esteem.
The online world has other dangers. Misinformation spreads quickly, especially when it appears in an entertaining meme or a confident-sounding podcast. Anonymous accounts make it easy for trolls to attack people without consequences.
In response, some users are choosing a "digital detox", deleting apps for a few weeks or limiting their screen time. Others follow accounts that share honest, unfiltered content. As one teenager put it, "I don't want perfect. I want real."
